strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored question at the intersection of NLP and qualitative data analysis: how collaboration modality (synchronous vs. asynchronous) affects human-in-the-loop (HitL) theme discovery systems.

Comprehensive experimental setup comparing three fundamentally different NLP paradigms (interactive topic modeling, relational learning, and LLM-prompted coding) across two contrasting domains (COVID-19 tweets and Facebook climate ads).
Multi-faceted evaluation framework that measures consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and post-hoc human-annotated correctness (1,200 sampled pairs with Krippendorff's alpha reported).
Complements quantitative findings with semi-structured interviews across 33 participants to offer practical design insights for interactive theme discovery systems.
weaknesses: The number of independent collaborative units per system is modest (three individual asynchronous coders and two 3-person synchronous groups per tool), which limits statistical power and raises questions about whether the t-test assumptions (e.g., independence across aligned theme pairs) strictly hold.

The LLM-based experiment relies on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, a relatively small parameter model. The conclusion that LLMs are inconsistent and struggle with scaling may be partly an artifact of using a 3B model rather than stronger open or proprietary models typically benchmarked for thematic coding.

As noted in the limitations, real-world asynchronous qualitative analysis almost always involves an explicit post-coding consolidation and reconciliation phase; evaluating individual async codebooks without consolidation creates an asymmetric comparison against synchronous groups that negotiate in real time.

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied research question: how collaborative modalities (synchronous vs. asynchronous) impact human-in-the-loop NLP systems for qualitative analysis and theme discovery.
Comprehensive comparative setup covering three representative paradigms of NLP-assisted qualitative coding: interactive topic models, relational structured inference, and LLM-based code propagation.

Well-structured evaluation framework covering consistency (Jaccard and embedding-based), cohesiveness and distinctiveness (intra- and inter-theme distances), and human-evaluated correctness across relatedness quartiles.
Rich mixed-methods analysis combining quantitative metrics with qualitative insights from semi-structured interviews and detailed dataset characteristics analysis.
weaknesses: Conflation of collaboration modality with group size: the synchronous setting involves 3 coders working together, whereas the asynchronous setting consists of individual coders working in isolation without a subsequent reconciliation/consolidation phase. In practice, asynchronous qualitative workflows typically incorporate multi-coder independent coding followed by structured consensus, making it hard to disentangle whether differences stem from real-time communication or simply group vs. individual cognitive effort.

Limited sample size and statistical power: each system-modality pair relies on only 2 synchronous runs and 3 asynchronous runs. Running t-tests across themes generated from such a small number of independent runs risks pseudoreplication, as themes within the same session/codebook are not independent observations.

Correctness analysis is restricted to only one dataset (COVID-19 tweets, Figure 4); presenting correctness results for the Climate dataset would have been crucial to validate whether the observed trends generalize across corpus types.

The choice of LLM (Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct) is relatively small for inductive reasoning and qualitative code assignment, which likely contributed heavily to the observed failure modes and high rates of unassigned documents (up to 16.1% in Table 10) compared to more capable models.

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied research question at the intersection of NLP and qualitative data analysis: how collaboration modalities (synchronous vs. asynchronous) impact human-in-the-loop (HitL) theme discovery systems.

Implements a multi-faceted evaluation framework that covers consistency across coder groups, intra/inter-theme cohesiveness and distinctiveness, and post-hoc manual validation of correctness with reported inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.632).

Covers a broad and representative spectrum of NLP paradigms (interactive topic modeling, relational structured learning, and LLM-based deductive coding) across two structurally and linguistically distinct datasets.

Involves a substantial human participant effort (33 researchers across 15 interactive sessions) complemented by semi-structured post-study interviews that yield actionable design insights for interactive NLP tools.
weaknesses: The experimental sample size at the group level is small (3 asynchronous coders and 2 synchronous groups per system). Performing two-sample t-tests at the theme level likely introduces pseudoreplication, as themes produced within the same session/codebook are not strictly independent observations.

The asynchronous setting omits the standard reconciliation/consolidation phase common in collaborative qualitative research (e.g., inter-coder agreement checking followed by group negotiation). Comparing individual asynchronous outputs directly to synchronously negotiated group codebooks creates a potential confound between the collaboration modality and the level of consensus consolidation.

The LLM condition relies solely on Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct. While computational constraints are understandable, a 3B parameter model is prone to substantial instruction-following and deductive classification errors (reflected in the high percentage of unlabeled/hallucinated outputs in Table 10), which limits how well the findings generalize to modern LLM-assisted qualitative workflows.

Correctness validation (Section 5.3 and Figure 4) is conducted only on the COVID dataset and omitted for the Climate dataset, leaving the correctness and robustness claims unverified across differing corpus characteristics.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in NLP-assisted qualitative research: evaluating interactive human-in-the-loop systems under different collaboration modalities (synchronous vs. asynchronous) rather than treating systems in isolation.

Comprehensive experimental design comparing three distinct technological paradigms (topic modeling, relational ILP/concept learning, and LLM prompting) across two structurally and linguistically contrasting corpora (COVID-19 tweets vs. Facebook climate ads).

Rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation framework that measures consistency (document overlap and embedding-space similarity), codebook cohesiveness and distinctiveness (intra- vs. inter-theme pairwise similarities), and correctness (manual post-hoc annotation of 2,400 instances with inter-annotator agreement reported).

Valuable practical takeaways connecting corpus characteristics (linguistic complexity, formulaic nature, semantic diversity) and interface affordances (richer manual interventions benefit more from real-time group deliberation) to system choice and collaboration setup.
weaknesses: Small sample size per experimental condition: each combination is tested with only 3 asynchronous individual coders and 2 synchronous groups (3 annotators each). While recruiting 33 researchers is commendable, having only N=2 or N=3 codebooks per cell limits statistical power and makes significance tests fragile to individual coder variance.

Potential participant/theme overlap across relational and LLM conditions: for the Climate Ads dataset, the theme sets reported in Table 15 (Relational) and Table 16 (LLM-based) contain virtually identical sets of theme names and identical counts (12, 17, 14, 25, 16), which strongly suggests reused codebooks or identical coder groups. The paper needs to explicitly clarify whether theme discovery in the LLM setting was conducted independently from scratch or derived from the relational setting.

Asynchronous collaboration setup is simplified: in traditional qualitative analysis workflows, asynchronous coding typically culminates in a reconciliation/consolidation phase where coders meet to negotiate a shared codebook. Evaluating raw individual codebooks against each other without this synthesis phase partially mischaracterizes standard asynchronous workflows.

The LLM baseline utilizes a relatively small model (Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct) which exhibits substantial classification limitations (e.g., generating unmapped labels or failing to reach high agreement), potentially underestimating the true capability of modern LLM-based interactive coding systems.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem at the intersection of NLP and qualitative data analysis: how collaboration dynamics (synchronous vs. asynchronous) impact interactive, NLP-assisted inductive coding tools.

Proposes a well-rounded and multifaceted evaluation framework covering consistency, cohesiveness & distinctiveness, and correctness, supported by both quantitative metrics and semi-structured qualitative interviews.
Compares three fundamentally different interactive paradigms (human-in-the-loop topic modeling, relational structured inference, and LLM prompting) over two structurally distinct datasets.

Substantial empirical investment involving 33 researchers/annotators across 30 experimental sessions and manual post-hoc validation of 2,400 document-theme pairs with reported inter-annotator agreement.
weaknesses: Confound between collaboration modality and group size: the synchronous setting involves 3 coders working together, whereas the asynchronous setting evaluates individual coders working in isolation. It is difficult to completely disentangle the effects of real-time deliberation from the sheer cognitive advantage of pooling three minds versus one, especially since typical asynchronous qualitative workflows involve independent coding followed by explicit reconciliation.

Small sample size of sessions per condition: each tool-dataset-modality combination relies on only 2 synchronous groups and 3 asynchronous individuals. Conducting t-tests over theme-level similarities across these few sessions risks violating independence assumptions and limits the statistical reliability of the comparisons.

Potential data duplication or reporting anomaly in the Appendix: the reported codebooks and theme counts in Table 15 (Relational, Climate Ads) and Table 16 (LLM-based, Climate Ads) appear virtually identical (with identical counts of 12, 17, 14, 25, 16 in Table 17), which requires clarification on whether codebooks were reused or if this is a copy-paste error.

The choice of LLM (Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct) is on the smaller side for complex semantic inductive coding and instruction following, which likely contributed to the high rate of unlabeled instances and unreliability observed at scale.
Visual readability issues in the Appendix figures: the labels in Figures 9, 10, and 11 are illegible even at high zoom levels.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored intersection between NLP systems and human-computer interaction: understanding how collaboration modalities (synchronous vs. asynchronous) impact human-in-the-loop qualitative text analysis.

Compares three distinct methodological paradigms for theme discovery (interactive topic modeling, relational/neuro-symbolic modeling, and LLM prompting) across two structurally and stylistically distinct datasets.

Presents a well-structured, multi-dimensional evaluation protocol assessing consistency across code-books, intra/inter-theme cohesiveness and distinctiveness, and post-hoc correctness with verified inter-annotator reliability (Krippendorff's alpha).

Complements quantitative findings with rich qualitative insights from semi-structured interviews of 33 researchers and extensive appendix documentation, including full code-books, prompts, and corpus-level linguistic analyses.
weaknesses: Conceptual conflation between individual coding and asynchronous collaboration: in standard qualitative research, asynchronous workflows involve independent coding followed by an asynchronous or structured reconciliation phase among multiple annotators. Here, the asynchronous condition consists of single individuals coding in isolation, making it difficult to disentangle the effect of collaboration modality from the effect of team size (1 coder vs. 3 coders).

Limited number of experimental sessions: each system-dataset condition is evaluated on only 3 asynchronous runs and 2 synchronous runs. While running 30 full coding sessions with 33 expert participants is resource-intensive, conducting two-sample t-tests over such small sample sizes risks low statistical power and susceptibility to individual coder idiosyncrasies.

The choice of LLM (Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct) is relatively small for inductive reasoning and zero/few-shot thematic labeling. State-of-the-art interactive LLM-assisted workflows typically leverage larger models (e.g., 70B+ parameters or frontier APIs), which may exhibit substantially different instruction-following and classification reliability at scale.
